confirmed.fix: (1) Fetch the course units, the course-wide passing set and the completions once per course and share them between the catalog, pass set and report (return the data from one helper instead of calling getLatestMarkedResultsForCourse twice). (2) Move the report to SQL: for each learner's target course (most recent enrolment via DISTINCT ON groupmember.created_at desc) compute passed_units / total_units with one grouped query over a CTE of non-exempt units x learners left-joined to a CTE of passing assessments. Buckets and averages become count(*) FILTER and avg. Only the at-risk list (inactive and < 100%) needs row-level output, with LIMIT/pagination. (3) Cache it (see 'overview-cache-weak'). (4) Decide the Manager behavior: either let the report use an org-wide internal function that does not hard-require ADMIN, or restrict the route to requireAdmin so it fails at the guard with a clear message.
confirmed.flow_risk: Admin Learners report and the Learner Progressions page share this code, so keep the output of getOrgProgression unchanged for that page. Edge cases: learners with zero enrolments (0%, 0/0), DEACTIVATED learners excluded, courseId filter drops learners not enrolled, units with several assessment items need every item passed (unit-level legacy rule when no tagged items), exempt units excluded via isNonGatingUnit. Opening the report to Managers must not widen what a Manager sees beyond the org-wide read-only list they already get elsewhere.
confirmed.verifier_note: Confirmed on both counts. (1) The Manager bug is real: reports.ts getLearnersReport runs assertManagerOrAdmin, which admits MANAGER, but then calls getOrgProgression (progression.ts:162-168), which throws 403 'Admins only' for any role other than ADMIN. The route /reports/learners (stats.ts:206) is requireManagerOrAdmin, so Managers get a 403 on a report they are meant to see. (2) The duplicate reads are real: progression.ts:236-243 runs buildCourseCatalog, buildCoursePassSet (getLatestMarkedResultsForCourse) AND getCourseProgressReport (which calls getOrderedUnitsForCourse and getLatestMarkedResultsForCourse again) per target course, so the course-wide DISTINCT ON and unit list run twice. All learners' ids go into 4 inArray queries.
confirmed.fix_adjustment: Fix the Manager 403 first (cheap, a correctness fix). Add an internal org-wide builder that accepts ADMIN or MANAGER (or let getOrgProgression accept MANAGER), and confirm the dashboard Learner Progressions page route still guards ADMIN if that is intended. Managers already see org-wide read-only data in the overview, so this does not widen access. Then dedupe the per-course reads by having getCourseProgressReport accept pre-fetched results or return them. Defer the SQL rewrite. Do not touch the tutor allocation-scoped getProgression path.

confirmed.title: Per-learner course progress and the completion rule run 2 sequential queries per unit; used on every learner home load, feedback-status poll and inside the marking transaction
confirmed.current: computeLearnerCourseProgress and isCourseComplete loop over every non-exempt unit and await hasLearnerPassedUnit, which does getAssessmentKeysForLesson (1 query) and then either getLatestMarkedResult or getLatestMarkedResultsByAssessment (1 query). That is about 2 x units sequential round trips per course. It is called for each enrolled course on the learner dashboard (dashboard.ts:121), the LMS-home overlay (enrolled-progress.ts:36), the tutor-feedback status check (tutor-feedback.ts:21, hit from the /lms layout on load) and recordCompletionIfComplete inside the recordResult transaction. Pure batched equivalents already exist: getLatestMarkedResultsForCourse and assembleReportRows (reports.ts), written for the admin report, but not used here.
confirmed.breaks_at: A 25-unit course is about 50 round trips (about 1-2.5 s at 20-50 ms pooler latency) per course per learner load. A learner with 3 courses on the home page: about 150 sequential queries, and the feedback-status call repeats it on every /lms layout mount. 1,000 concurrent learners is about 150k queries/min against a 10-connection pool. In the marking path the transaction connection is held for the full chain, so tutors marking in bursts exhaust the pool.
confirmed.fix: Add getLatestMarkedResultsForLearnerCourse(learnerId, courseId) (single DISTINCT ON query filtered by learner_id and course_id) plus getAssessmentKeysByLesson(unitIds) (already exists), and compute passed per unit in memory using the same isUnitPassed logic as assembleReportRows. That makes it 3 queries per course regardless of unit count. Better: a getLearnerProgressForCourses(learnerId, courseIds[]) that does it for all courses in 3 queries, so the home page costs 3 queries total. Keep a single shared pure rule (the existing computeProgress) so learner and manager numbers cannot diverge. The tutor-feedback status check can then derive passedUnits from the same batched read, or from a count of passing verdicts, instead of full course progress.
confirmed.flow_risk: Touches learner dashboard, My Learning, tutor feedback prompt, the completion trigger and the sequential-unlock guard (services/gating/unlock.ts:35, guards/ownership.ts:218 use the same per-unit helper). The completion trigger must still read within the same tx so it sees the just-recorded Pass (read-your-writes), so pass the tx client into the batched query. The existing tests (completion, progress, marking) lock current behaviour; add a parity test against hasLearnerPassedUnit for legacy units (assessment_key NULL), multi-item units, refers followed by passes, and drafts that must be ignored (only final+verdict counts).
confirmed.verifier_note: Confirmed. progress.ts:80-94 and completion.ts:29-41 loop over non-exempt units and await hasLearnerPassedUnit, which does getAssessmentKeysForLesson and then one more query (coursework.ts:459-471). That is about 2 x units sequential round trips per course. It is called per enrolled course from lms/dashboard.ts:121, enrolled-progress.ts:36 and tutor-feedback.ts computePassedUnits (hit from the lms.ts:42 route, which the /lms layout calls), and inside the recordResult transaction via recordCompletionIfComplete. This is the most learner-facing issue on the list: it hits every learner page load, not just admins. getLatestMarkedResultsForCourse and getAssessmentKeysByLesson already exist as batched building blocks.
confirmed.fix_adjustment: Correct approach, with one caution. A per-learner batched read must reproduce hasLearnerPassedUnit exactly: for a unit with tagged assessment keys every key needs a passing latest FINAL verdict; for an untagged unit, the legacy per-lesson latest marked result. Note the batched DISTINCT ON groups by (learner, lesson, assessment_key), so the legacy NULL-key case maps cleanly. Pass the tx client into the batched call inside recordCompletionIfComplete for read-your-writes. Make the tutor-feedback status check reuse the same batched call. Add parity tests (NULL key, multi-item, refer then pass, drafts ignored). The same per-unit helper is also used by the unlock guard (gating/unlock.ts) and the ownership guard, so migrate those separately and carefully.

confirmed.title: Last-seen lookups send all learner IDs to two scanning queries (login events + sessions) and are repeated per tutor
confirmed.current: getLastSeenForUserIds(ids) runs MAX(logged_in_at) GROUP BY user over analytics_login_events and MAX(updated_at) GROUP BY user over session, each filtered with inArray over every id. The session table has no user_id index (schema.ts:113-130; only the token unique index), so each call scans the whole session table. It is called once org-wide in the overview, once more inside the org-wide computePipelineForRoster, then once per tutor via computePipelineForRoster, and once more per progression or learner-report view. Errors are swallowed and return an all-null map, which silently turns every learner into 'never logged in'.
confirmed.breaks_at: session grows with every login and every refresh (session updated_at is already written about 33k times in prod). At 10k learners with several sessions each, each call scans 10^5 rows, and there are 2 + tutors of them per overview. A failure under load (timeout) silently misclassifies all learners as neverLoggedIn.
confirmed.fix: (1) Add CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY on session(user_id, updated_at DESC) and keep analytics_login_events(user_id, logged_in_at). (2) Compute in SQL for the org: a lateral/aggregate over organizationmember (STUDENT) left-joined to the per-user max, and return only counts for 7d/30d/never buckets, not a Map of ids. (3) Better, add profile.last_seen_at (or reuse the login-event row) updated at most once per few minutes in the existing session-refresh path, so 'active/inactive/never' becomes a plain indexed column on profile and no session scan is ever needed. (4) On failure, throw or return 'unknown' rather than null (null is indistinguishable from never logged in).
confirmed.flow_risk: Affects the activity buckets on the admin overview, tutor pipeline stats, progression 'created/active/inactive' and at-risk lists. Definition to preserve: lastSeen = the later of last login event and last session update; >30 days = inactive; none = created/never. A denormalized column needs a backfill from existing data, and the writer must not add load to the hot auth path (throttle the write). DEACTIVATED handling stays in the status map.
confirmed.verifier_note: Confirmed. analytics.ts getLastSeenForUserIds runs MAX() GROUP BY over analytics_login_events (which has an idx on user_id) and over session. session (schema.ts:113-130) has no user_id or updated_at index, only the unique token index. It is called org-wide in the overview, again inside the org pipeline and once per tutor via computePipelineForRoster. The catch block returns an all-null map, which silently turns every learner into 'never logged in'. All verified. Severity is medium: the session table is small today and the query is not user-facing.
confirmed.fix_adjustment: Add session(user_id) ONLY. Do NOT add an index on session.updated_at or (user_id, updated_at): better-auth writes updated_at often (~33k writes in prod), and indexing that column disables HOT updates, adding bloat and write amplification on the hottest auth table. A user_id index is enough, since user_id never changes. Make the swallowed error visible (rethrow, or return a flagged 'unknown') so a failure is not read as 'never logged in'. Avoid the denormalised profile.last_seen_at column for now; it puts a write on the hot auth path. De-duplicate calls instead: compute the org last-seen map once per overview and reuse it for the per-tutor pipelines.

confirmed.title: Missing/misaligned indexes behind the report and dashboard queries
confirmed.location: packages/db/src/schema.ts:113-130 (session), groupmember unique(group_id, profile_id) ~1320, organizationmember ~indexes, course_section, lesson, message_thread/message (schema.ts:4265-4293), coursework_submission indexes (migration 0011:43-44); queries at packages/db/src/queries/caseload/dashboard.ts:19-95, dash/admin-overview.ts:54-60,276-298,367-396,421-436
confirmed.current: Verified missing from the schema and migrations: session(user_id) and session(updated_at) (last-seen + online-now); groupmember(profile_id, role_id) (getCoursesForLearners, getEnrolmentsForLearners and the isAllocatedTutor course checks filter profile_id IN (...) and role_id = 3, but the only multi-column keys lead with group_id); course_section(course_id) (getLessonCoursePairs, getLessonIdsForCourses); lesson(section_id); organizationmember(organization_id, role_id) (every roster/count query; only single-column org and profile indexes exist); message_thread(organization_id) and message(created_at) (getOrgMessagingStats joins thread->message filtered by the last 7 days); coursework_submission has (learner_id, lesson_id) and (course_id) but the course-wide DISTINCT ON (getLatestMarkedResultsForCourse) needs (course_id, learner_id, lesson_id, assessment_key, version DESC) filtered to submission_type='final' to avoid a sort; unit_time_monthly uses year_month LIKE 'YYYY-%' (non-sargable on text). Supabase advisor also reports 103 unindexed foreign keys and 74 unused indexes.
confirmed.breaks_at: All of these are cheap with 40 learners and become sequential scans plus sorts per request at tens of thousands of rows in session/groupmember/coursework_submission/message. The online-now poll (every 45s per open admin tab) scans session each time.
confirmed.fix: One migration with CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY IF NOT EXISTS (via the session pooler :5432, not in a transaction): session(user_id, updated_at DESC); groupmember(profile_id, role_id) INCLUDE (group_id); organizationmember(organization_id, role_id) INCLUDE (profile_id); course_section(course_id); lesson(section_id); message_thread(organization_id); message(created_at); coursework_submission(course_id, learner_id, lesson_id, assessment_key, version DESC) WHERE submission_type='final'. Change unit_time_monthly filters to year_month >= 'YYYY-01' AND < 'YYYY+1-01'. Cross-check against the 74 unused indexes list before adding, and drop the redundant single-column ones that these cover.
confirmed.flow_risk: No query semantics change. Risks: write amplification on session (written very frequently; keep the index narrow) and on coursework_submission; CONCURRENTLY builds on prod are slow but non-blocking; do not run inside a drizzle migration transaction. Run EXPLAIN on prod copies of the 5-6 hottest queries before and after.
confirmed.verifier_note: Partly confirmed. Verified missing in schema.ts and the migrations: session(user_id); groupmember(profile_id, ...) (only the unique (group_id, profile_id) and the unique_entries keys, none leading with profile_id); course_section(course_id); lesson(section_id) (only idx_lesson_course_slug (course_id, slug)); message_thread(organization_id). Overstated or wrong: message(created_at) is not needed, because idx_message_thread_created (thread_id, created_at) already exists and the join goes thread to message; organizationmember(organization_id, role_id) is marginal because single-column organization and profile indexes exist and there is 1 org; the unit_time_monthly LIKE 'YYYY-%' prefix is trivial on a tiny table. A unit_time_monthly rewrite buys nothing.
confirmed.fix_adjustment: Keep the list to: session(user_id); groupmember(profile_id) INCLUDE (group_id, role_id) (these also help isAllocatedTutor and getCoursesForLearners); course_section(course_id); lesson(section_id); message_thread(organization_id); and maybe a partial coursework_submission(course_id, learner_id, lesson_id, assessment_key, version DESC) WHERE submission_type='final'. Drop session(updated_at) from the proposal (HOT loss, see last-seen-lookup). Run CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY via a separate session-pooler (:5432) script, since drizzle migrations run in a transaction. Check pg_stat_user_indexes before adding or dropping anything. This is the cheapest high-value item and pairs with the 103 unindexed FK advisor warning.

confirmed.title: Online-now panel polls an uncached join over session every 45 seconds per open admin tab
confirmed.current: getOnlineOrgMembers joins session x profile x organizationmember with updated_at >= cutoff, group by profile/role, ordered by max(updated_at). It has no cache, no row limit, and returns every online user with name and email. The client sets setInterval(45000) with no visibility check, so background tabs keep polling. Because session.updated_at is bumped on every refresh, this table also carries the write pressure.
confirmed.breaks_at: A few hundred concurrent learners returns hundreds of rows per poll, and a table scan on session (no updated_at index) per poll per admin tab. With 5 managers/admins that is about 7 polls/min against a heavy query forever, even when nobody is looking.
confirmed.fix: Add the session(updated_at) index (see report-indexes). Add a 15-20s shared cache (Redis or in-process single-flight) because the data is the same for all admins. Cap the returned user list (for example the 50 most recent, count and byRole computed in SQL with count(*) FILTER). Pause polling when document.hidden and back off to 2-3 minutes. Optionally replace the DB read with a Redis sorted set (ZADD presence:{org} now userId on the existing session-touch path, ZCOUNT by window).
confirmed.flow_risk: Admin and manager dashboard only. The count and byRole must stay exact, so compute them in SQL rather than from the truncated list. 'Online' = session refreshed within 5 minutes; a Redis presence set must apply the same window and be skipped gracefully when Redis is down (existing logRedisUnavailableOnce pattern).
confirmed.verifier_note: Confirmed. getOnlineOrgMembers (queries/dash/admin-overview.ts:309-332) joins session, profile and organizationmember with no limit and no cache. The count and byRole are computed in JS from the returned rows (services/dash/admin-overview.ts:344-364). The client polls every 45s with no document.hidden check (admin-dashboard.svelte:36-44). The session table is small and filtered by recent updated_at, so the cost is low until hundreds of sessions are active at once.
confirmed.fix_adjustment: Pause polling on document.hidden and use a short (15-20s) single-flight cache; both are trivial. Do NOT index session.updated_at (HOT loss). Keep count/byRole exact by computing them in SQL if the user list is capped. Skip the Redis presence set for now.

confirmed.title: getCourseStats multiplies students x lessons x completions in one join with COUNT(DISTINCT), and 'top courses' is sorted ascending
confirmed.current: For each course the query left-joins groupmember (students) and independently left-joins lesson, then lessonCompletion on both. That yields S x L rows per course, de-duplicated with COUNT(DISTINCT ...) FILTER. The outer query orders by completedLessons ascending and takes limit(5), so 'topCourses' returns the five LEAST completed courses. getOrganisationAnalytics runs it plus three more queries with no cache on every call. getTotalCertificatesIssued and getRecentCertifications also join groupmember x course per request.
confirmed.breaks_at: S x L rows per course: 5,000 students x 40 lessons is 200k rows per course before the distinct, repeated for every ACTIVE course, with a sort over the aggregated rows. Grows with both learners and course length.
confirmed.fix: Pre-aggregate independently and join on course id: students = count(*) from groupmember (role 3) by group; lessons = count(*) from lesson by course; completed_lessons = count(*) of lesson_completion joined to lesson by course filtered to is_complete; certificates = count(*) FILTER on certificate_earned_at. Combine as three small grouped subqueries joined by course_id. Order by a meaningful metric (enrolments desc) if 'top' is intended. Cache the whole OrganisationAnalytics in Redis for a few minutes (the org page is shown to all roles on load).
confirmed.flow_risk: Feeds the org stats widget (/dash/stats). Changing the ORDER BY changes visible output, so confirm with the owner whether 'top' should mean most-enrolled. Count semantics: completion% is completed_lessons / (students x lessons); keep that formula. Only ACTIVE courses are included. Compliance courses use a separate completion mechanism, so they are unaffected.
confirmed.verifier_note: Confirmed. dash.ts:22-72 left-joins groupmember and lesson independently, then lessonCompletion, which gives S x L rows per course. It de-duplicates with COUNT(DISTINCT) and orders ascending by completedLessons with limit 5, so 'topCourses' returns the five LEAST completed. It is uncached in getOrganisationAnalytics. Real and unbounded in S x L, but only for ACTIVE courses and only on the org stats widget.
confirmed.fix_adjustment: Pre-aggregate students, lessons and completions in three grouped subqueries joined on course_id. Keep the completion% formula completed_lessons / (students x lessons). The ORDER BY direction is a visible product decision: confirm with the owner before flipping it, or keep the ascending order and rename it. Note lessonCompletion joins on profileId = groupmember.profileId, so count completions per course filtered to enrolled students (role 3) to keep the numerator equal to today's.

confirmed.title: Overview runs duplicated or non-sargable aggregate queries and loads full rosters just for counts
confirmed.current: (1) getTimeToCompleteStats runs the same 4-table join twice (per course and overall). getCompletionStats runs two queries (byCourse, then this-month). getCertificateStats runs two. (2) getEnrollmentTrend, getSubmissionsOverTime and getCompletionsTrend filter with extract(year from col) = $year, which prevents index use, and group by extract(month ...). getOrgStudyHoursMonthly filters year_month LIKE. (3) listOrgLearners does selectDistinct with a name sort over the entire student roster, returning id, name and email for every learner, but the overview needs only count, ids for last-seen, and an ID-status tally. (4) getCourseEnrolledLearnerIds returns one row per (course, learner) over the whole org so Node can intersect with the last-seen map for 'active 30d' per course. (5) getLessonCoursePairs + getAssessmentItemsByLesson load lesson.documents jsonb for every lesson in the org to count assessments. (6) getOrgCoursesWithEnrolment uses count(distinct ...) over groupmember joined per course.
confirmed.breaks_at: Each is modest alone, but together about 12 org-wide scans per cache miss; (3) and (4) transfer O(learners x courses) rows to Node and (5) transfers every lesson's full documents array. Fine at 40 learners, noticeable at 10k+.
confirmed.fix: Use ROLLUP/GROUPING SETS (or FILTER aggregates in one pass) to merge the paired queries; change year filters to range predicates (col >= make_date(year,1,1) AND col < make_date(year+1,1,1)) and group by date_trunc('month'); compute per-course active-30d in SQL by joining groupmember to a per-user last-seen subquery (or profile.last_seen_at from 'last-seen-lookup'); compute per-course assessment counts in SQL with jsonb_array_elements over lesson.documents (filtered to the assessment kinds, by course); compute ID verification not_verified with a count instead of reading the roster. Stop calling listOrgLearners from the overview once the pipeline moves to SQL.
confirmed.flow_risk: Dashboard numbers only. Edge cases: months with no data are zero-filled by fillMonths (keep); time zones (extract on timestamp without tz versus UTC year in Node: keep UTC and the same boundary); a learner enrolled in several courses counts once org-wide but once per course in per-course tables; deleted courses (status DELETED) excluded everywhere; assessment kinds must go through the same isAssessmentKind rule as getAssessmentItemsByLesson.
confirmed.verifier_note: Largely confirmed. extract(year from col) = $year is used at admin-overview.ts queries lines 125, 243 and 268. The paired queries in getCompletionStats, getTimeToCompleteStats and getCertificateStats run twice. listOrgLearners does a selectDistinct with a name sort over the whole student roster. These are modest costs, each a single org-scoped scan, so low severity. They only matter in aggregate, and most disappear once the pipeline stops loading the roster.
confirmed.fix_adjustment: Convert year filters to range predicates only if a time-based index exists (none is claimed); otherwise this changes nothing. Do the merge-paired-queries work only when touching those functions anyway. Keep the UTC year boundary identical (timestamp columns vs withTimezone). Low priority; do not make it a standalone project.

confirmed.title: Referrals report streams every final submission verdict in the org into Node to count open refers; four org-wide queries per view, unbounded output
confirmed.current: getLearnerOpenReferCounts runs DISTINCT ON (learner, lesson, assessment_key) over all final submissions with a verdict in the org and returns one row per assessment, then counts non-PASS in a JS loop. getLearnerLastReferral does a DISTINCT ON over every refer row org-wide. The tutor and learner breakdowns scan the same coursework_result/submission/course/group join twice more. The service returns one row per learner who was ever referred with no pagination. The query hardcodes result <> 'PASS' while the app uses isPassingResult/PASSING_RESULTS, so the two can drift if a second passing value is added.
confirmed.breaks_at: Rows read equals total verdicts in the org (about 10^5 at a few thousand learners) per view, from an uncached endpoint.
confirmed.fix: Do the open-refer count in SQL: wrap the DISTINCT ON in a subquery and SELECT learner_id, count(*) FILTER (WHERE result <> 'PASS') GROUP BY learner_id (pass the passing set as an array parameter, result <> ALL($1)). Fold the four queries into two with CTEs sharing one scan. Paginate or cap perLearner (server-side sort and limit plus a total) and cache for a few minutes (admin only).
confirmed.flow_risk: Admin-only Referrals report. Keep the definition: a refer is a verdict that is not passing, counted across all versions; 'open' = the latest final verdict per (learner, lesson, assessment_key) is still a refer; 'Removed grader' bucket for recorded_by IS NULL. The ADMIN-only check must stay before any cache read.
confirmed.verifier_note: Confirmed with an overstatement. getLearnerOpenReferCounts (queries/dash/admin-overview.ts ~570-620) does DISTINCT ON (learner, lesson, assessment_key) in SQL, so rows transferred are one per assessment, not every verdict as claimed. The JS loop then counts non-PASS. The hardcoded result <> 'PASS' (lines 477-482 and ~543) duplicates isPassingResult, which the source itself documents. perLearner is unbounded and the endpoint is uncached. The report is admin-only and infrequently viewed. It is a legitimate drift risk and a mild scale cost.
confirmed.fix_adjustment: Wrap the DISTINCT ON in a subquery and count with FILTER in SQL, passing PASSING_RESULTS as a parameter instead of the literal 'PASS'. That removes the JS loop and the drift risk in one small change. Keep requireAdmin before any cache. Pagination is optional.

confirmed.title: Activity log report fetches up to 2,000 full rows (including stack/message) a second time just to count, and severity totals describe only the limited page
confirmed.current: getSystemEventsReport calls getSystemEvents for the filtered page (default 500, max 2000) and computes bySeverity from that capped page, so totals.total is the page size, not the real total. It then calls getSystemEvents again with limit 2000 and select() of all columns (message, stack) and filters it in JS to count errors and failed logins in the last 24h. Retention purge deleteSystemEventsOlderThan deletes with .returning({id}) and counts the array length, which materializes every deleted id in Node. system_event_log grows with every login/logout/API error, and has 5 single-column indexes plus the org+time one (write amplification on every request that logs).
confirmed.breaks_at: Under an error storm (a failing dependency generating thousands of rows/min) the KPI call transfers 2,000 rows of stack text every time an admin opens the page, and the first purge after a long gap returns a huge id array. The page's severity totals will silently be wrong once there are more rows than the limit.
confirmed.fix: Replace the second fetch with SELECT count(*) FILTER (WHERE severity='error'), count(*) FILTER (WHERE event_type='auth.login.failure') FROM system_event_log WHERE organization_id=$1 AND occurred_at >= now()-interval '24h'. Compute bySeverity and total with a grouped count using the same WHERE as the page (and keep the page LIMIT). Make the purge a loop of DELETE ... WHERE id IN (SELECT id ... LIMIT 5000) returning only the count (or use the rowCount), and drop the unused single-column indexes (event_type, severity, occurred_at, user_email) if the advisor confirms they are unused.
confirmed.flow_risk: Admin-only Activity log page. Totals will change meaning from 'rows in page' to 'rows matching the filter' (more correct); confirm the UI labels. The purge job in apps/jobs must be re-tested. Index drops should be checked against pg_stat_user_indexes first.
confirmed.verifier_note: Confirmed, and it is a correctness bug as well as a scale issue. system-events.ts:31-41 computes bySeverity and totals.total from the filtered page (so total = page size, not the real count). It then fetches up to 2000 FULL rows (message, stack) a second time and counts errors and failed logins in JS. Past 2000 events in 24h the errorsLast24h and failedLoginsLast24h KPIs are silently capped at 2000. deleteSystemEventsOlderThan (queries/system-events:~96-103) uses .returning({id}), so the first purge after a gap materialises every deleted id in Node. The log table grows with every login and API error.
confirmed.fix_adjustment: Replace the second fetch with a single count(*) FILTER query on organization_id and occurred_at >= now()-24h; compute severity totals with a grouped count that shares the page's WHERE. Make the purge delete in batches (DELETE ... WHERE id IN (SELECT id ... LIMIT 5000)) and return the row count rather than ids. Keep the maintenance job's retention behaviour identical. Do not drop indexes without checking pg_stat_user_indexes.

confirmed.title: Several report and roster endpoints return unbounded lists, and some do O(n x m) lookups in JS
confirmed.current: getOrgTutorFeedback returns every feedback entry (including free-text comments) with no limit, and the report also returns them all in entries[]. The per-course progress report returns a row for every enrolled learner; listAllocationsByOrg returns every allocation; getCourseComplianceOverview returns every learner in the course; the learners-report atRisk list is unbounded. getTutorCaseload (ADMIN path, org-wide roster) calls roster.find(...) inside the loop over awaiting items, which is O(awaiting x roster). Frontend CSV export (export-csv.ts) is built client-side from these arrays, so there is no server-side streaming or paging.
confirmed.breaks_at: Payload size and browser render time grow linearly with learners x feedback milestones: 10k learners x several milestones is tens of thousands of rows in a single JSON response and DOM. The O(n x m) loop is quadratic in the admin caseload page: 1,000 awaiting x 5,000 roster is 5M comparisons per request.
confirmed.fix: Add server-side pagination (limit/cursor/total) to the tutor-feedback entries, allocations, progress report and at-risk list; keep the aggregates (averages, per-tutor) computed in SQL with avg()/count() GROUP BY tutor_id so they stay exact. For exports, add a streaming CSV endpoint (hono stream, keyset pagination in chunks of 1-2k rows) instead of assembling arrays in the browser or the API. Replace roster.find with a Map<learnerId, name> built once.
confirmed.flow_risk: The dashboard tables (tutor-feedback-report, learner-progressions, course-overview-table, tutor-performance-table) currently assume the full array, so they need page controls and server-side filtering/sorting before the API can be capped, otherwise totals and 'select all' behaviours silently change. Streaming exports must keep the same role guards (admin/manager) and the allocation scoping for tutors, and use the same column set and PII allow-list (the per-course report deliberately excludes profile PII).
confirmed.verifier_note: Confirmed in part. getOrgTutorFeedback (tutor-feedback.ts:66-87) has no limit. roster.find inside the awaiting loop (caseload.ts:127) is O(awaiting x roster) and applies to tutors as well as the admin path. Per-course progress reports return a row per enrolled learner. Real but low: payload size and render time, not DB load, and tutor rosters are small. Pagination requires front-end changes to several tables and exports, so the change cost is high relative to the current benefit.
confirmed.fix_adjustment: Do the roster.find to Map change now (trivial, zero risk). Defer pagination and streaming CSV until a table actually becomes slow. Any pagination needs server-side sort and filter first, or 'select all' and totals silently change.

confirmed.title: Images are built ON the 4 GB prod droplet: 20-45 min of CPU/RAM starvation, OOM risk, no registry rollback
confirmed.current: `docker compose up -d --build` builds api, dashboard and jobs from source on the same box that serves traffic. Compose builds the three images in parallel. The dashboard build runs vite with NODE_OPTIONS=--max-old-space-size=8072 (8 GB heap on a 4 GB host). Each image does its own `pnpm fetch` + install of the monorepo. Rollback is `git checkout <hash>` plus another full rebuild. The only publish pipeline (docker-publish.yml) is manual-dispatch and pointed at ClassroomIO's Docker Hub, so nothing is pushed to a registry we control.
confirmed.breaks_at: Already hurts today (20-45 min of degraded site per deploy). With thousands of learners, every deploy lands during teaching hours. A parallel 3-image build plus live traffic on 2 vCPU/4 GB can trigger the kernel OOM killer. The killer can pick redis, caddy or a running api, which drops queued jobs and causes an outage rather than just slowness. A rollback takes another 20-45 min, so a bad release means a long outage.
confirmed.fix: Build in CI and deploy by pulling. (1) Re-enable a GitHub Actions workflow that builds the 3 images with buildx plus GHA cache and pushes to GHCR, tagged with the git SHA (keeps the AGPL deployed==pushed rule: the tag is the commit). Fix the smoke job to use the ephemeral postgres service, which it already declares. (2) On the droplet, replace `build:` with `image: ghcr.io/integer-training/pearl-<svc>:${IMAGE_TAG}` and deploy with `docker compose pull && docker compose up -d`. (3) Rollback becomes `IMAGE_TAG=<prev> docker compose up -d`, which takes seconds. (4) Until then, add `--build` serialization (`COMPOSE_PARALLEL_LIMIT=1`), 4 GB swap, and cut --max-old-space-size to about 3072. Cost: $0 (GHCR/Actions free tier).
confirmed.flow_risk: No functional flow changes. Risks: the dashboard bakes PUBLIC_IS_SELFHOSTED=true at build time, so the CI build arg must match. Env-specific PUBLIC_* values must not be baked in. Private-registry login is needed on the droplet (read-only PAT). Keep the sha tag in the DEPLOY.md record so AGPL traceability is not lost. Admin, tutor, learner and manager flows are unaffected, and they benefit because the site stays fast during deploys.
confirmed.verifier_note: Confirmed. Compose uses build: for api, dashboard and jobs and DEPLOY.md runs `up -d --build`. Dockerfile.dashboard sets NODE_OPTIONS=--max-old-space-size=8072. Each Dockerfile does its own pnpm fetch. Rollback is `git checkout` plus a rebuild (DEPLOY.md:100). docker-publish.yml is workflow_dispatch only, with the smoke job commented as broken. Not critical: this is deploy-time degradation, not a standing fault. The OOM claim is unproven. REPLICATION.md D13/K13 says Pearl's sibling droplet has 4 GB swap, and the docs assume sequential builds. DEPLOY.md and RUNBOOK.md do not record that Pearl has swap, so check with `swapon --show` on the droplet before asserting 'no swap'.
confirmed.fix_adjustment: Direction is correct and worth doing first. Make the CI build arg PUBLIC_IS_SELFHOSTED=true match Dockerfile.dashboard. No other PUBLIC_* values are baked in today. Use a read-only deploy token or a public GHCR package, and tag with the git SHA. Cheaper interim step: COMPOSE_PARALLEL_LIMIT=1 and cutting the 8072 heap cap to about 3072. Do not drop the AGPL rule that the deployed image equals the pushed commit.

confirmed.title: Deploy and restart path has guaranteed downtime: fixed container_names, migrations on api boot, no upstream retry in Caddy
confirmed.current: `up -d` stops the old api and dashboard, then starts the new ones. A new api first runs `pnpm --filter @cio/db db:setup` (roles, advisory lock, baseline, drizzle migrate, essential seed) on EVERY boot, then `pnpm start`, so it is unhealthy for roughly 30-90 s. The dashboard has `depends_on: api: service_healthy` but no healthcheck of its own. Caddy has `depends_on: dashboard` with no condition and no `lb_try_duration` / `health_uri`, so while the dashboard or api is down users get immediate 502s. `container_name` on every service makes `--scale` and blue/green impossible. Migrations run inside the app container with the app's start_period (40 s + 12x10 s).
confirmed.breaks_at: Every deploy or crash-restart is a visible outage window of about 1-2 min, and active exam or coursework submissions in that window fail. A slow migration (for example the 103 FK indexes the advisor flags) makes the api look unhealthy for minutes. At 20k learners a restart during peak hits thousands of users.
confirmed.fix: (1) Remove container_name and add a one-shot `migrate` service (same api image, command `pnpm --filter @cio/db db:setup`, restart: 'no'); api and dashboard `depends_on: migrate: service_completed_successfully`, and set SKIP_DB_SETUP=true on api. (2) Run api and dashboard as 2 replicas each using a rollout pattern (docker-rollout plugin, or `--scale api=2 --no-recreate`, then remove the old containers). (3) Caddy: `reverse_proxy { dynamic a { name dashboard port 3082 } lb_try_duration 30s lb_try_interval 250ms health_uri /healthz health_interval 5s }` so restarts are retried rather than 502'd. (4) Make migrations expand/contract only (additive), because old replicas keep serving while migrations run. (5) Add a dashboard healthcheck.
confirmed.flow_risk: Replicas require every in-memory state to be Redis-backed. The API is mostly stateless, but Better Auth's rate limiter is in-memory (see auth-ratelimit-memory-per-process) and the custom-domain origin registry is per process. The dashboard calls `http://api:3081` and Node fetch keep-alive pins connections to one replica, so use Caddy or an internal LB hop rather than Docker DNS round-robin. Migrations that drop or rename columns would break the old replicas during the overlap, so they need a two-step release. All roles share these paths, and tutor allocation filtering (ACCESS.md section 8) is unaffected.
confirmed.verifier_note: Facts confirmed. container_name is set on every service. entrypoint-api.sh runs db:setup on every boot, including runSeedEssential outside the shouldSyncSchema guard. The dashboard has no healthcheck. Caddy has plain `reverse_proxy dashboard:3082` with no retry, and `depends_on: dashboard` with no condition. Impact is a roughly 1-2 min 502 window per deploy. That is real but tolerable at today's scale, so medium. The healthcheck window is 40s + 12x10s, so a slow migration only delays the dashboard start. It does not cause kills.
confirmed.fix_adjustment: Do the cheap steps first. (a) Caddy `lb_try_duration 30s` and `lb_try_interval 250ms` work with a single upstream. (b) A separate one-shot `migrate` service with SKIP_DB_SETUP=true on api; entrypoint-api.sh already supports that variable. (c) A dashboard healthcheck. Defer 2-replica rollouts until the stateless issues are fixed. In-memory Better Auth throttles and the per-process origin registry are not replica-safe. The dashboard-to-api hop on `http://api:3081` also needs sticky or LB handling. The tutor allocation rule is unaffected.

confirmed.title: No memory/CPU limits or Node heap caps on any container: one leak or ffmpeg spike OOM-kills the whole box
confirmed.current: redis, api, dashboard, jobs and caddy have no mem_limit, memory reservation, cpus or `--max-old-space-size`. Node picks its heap from host RAM. jobs runs media (ffmpeg probe/thumbnail/audio extraction/transcode, concurrency 2), transcribe, emails, notifications, maintenance and agent course-generation in one process (apps/jobs/src/index.ts:3-8). Redis has no maxmemory.
confirmed.breaks_at: As soon as a few large video uploads are processed concurrently with SSR traffic, ffmpeg plus 6 workers can take 1-2 GB and push the host into swap or the OOM killer. The killer may take down redis (queue loss), caddy or dockerd rather than the offender. A dashboard leak under load does the same. Failure is whole-site, not one service.
confirmed.fix: Set budgets that fit 4 GB (then scale with the droplet): redis mem_limit 320m; api 768m with NODE_OPTIONS=--max-old-space-size=576; dashboard 768m (heap 576); jobs 1200m (heap 768); caddy 128m. Add cpus: '1.0' on jobs and set ffmpeg `-threads 1` / `nice` so media work cannot starve SSR. Split media and transcribe into a separate `jobs-media` service (same image, `CMD node apps/jobs/dist/workers/media.js`, as the Dockerfile comment already suggests), so emails, notifications and maintenance never share fate with ffmpeg. Add `oom_score_adj` for redis/caddy and a 4 GB swapfile (DEPLOY.md does not mention swap, although the replication notes call it mandatory).
confirmed.flow_risk: Too tight a heap cap makes a legitimate large job (big docx, a long video) crash, so retune after watching `docker stats` for a week. A jobs-media split means two jobs-type containers; the maintenance and notification schedulers use idempotent upsertJobScheduler, so duplicate boots are safe. Learner uploads/transcription and tutor marking depend on jobs, so keep BullMQ retries on.
confirmed.verifier_note: Confirmed. No mem_limit, cpus or NODE_OPTIONS on any service, and Redis has no maxmemory. All six workers run in one jobs process, with media concurrency 2, ffmpeg, transcribe, emails and agent generation. The 'OOM killer may pick redis or caddy' claim is overstated. The kernel kills by oom_score, so it usually picks the largest node or ffmpeg process. Container memory limits do reduce blast radius and are the right fix. 'Whole-box' failure is plausible but unproven. Medium, not high.
confirmed.fix_adjustment: The numbers are only a starting point. Observe `docker stats` first, because a 576 MB heap cap on SSR or the api could crash on legitimate peaks. Add -threads 1 to ffmpeg (apps/jobs/src/utils/ffmpeg.ts has no thread or nice flags). Splitting jobs-media into its own service is the best structural change, but the Dockerfile.jobs comment implies per-worker entrypoints may need verifying. Confirm swap exists before relying on it.

confirmed.title: Unbounded Docker json-file logs plus per-request console.log noise
confirmed.location: docker-compose.deploy.yaml (no logging: block); apps/api/src/app.ts:94 (hono logger on every request); apps/api/src/utils/origins.ts:17; apps/dashboard/src/lib/utils/services/auth/session.ts:15,44; apps/dashboard/src/lib/utils/services/auth/server.ts:11; apps/dashboard/src/hooks.server.ts:156
confirmed.current: No service sets a `logging:` driver or max-size/max-file, so Docker uses json-file with NO rotation. The api logs one line per request (logger()), `console.log('check origin', origin)` fires on every CORS check, and the dashboard SSR logs 'baseURL' and 'has locals' on every page and session check. DEPLOY.md and RUNBOOK.md only mention `docker compose logs`, and nothing about rotation.
confirmed.breaks_at: Log volume scales linearly with requests: thousands of learners at about 5-20 req/s is several GB/day of text on the same disk as images and the Docker root. A full disk makes dockerd, caddy and redis AOF writes fail, which is a full outage. Growth also makes `docker compose logs | grep correlationId` (the documented incident workflow) slow.
confirmed.fix: Add a YAML anchor `x-logging: &logging {driver: json-file, options: {max-size: '20m', max-file: '5'}}` and apply it to all services (or set it globally in /etc/docker/daemon.json). Delete the 5 stray console.log lines. Make hono `logger()` conditional (skip /health and static; sample 2xx) or switch to a structured logger. For search, ship logs off-box (Grafana Cloud/Loki free tier, or Better Stack free).
confirmed.flow_risk: Near-zero. Logs are only read manually during incidents. Keep correlationId lines intact, since the RUNBOOK relies on them. Rotating logs loses history older than max-size x max-file, which is acceptable once error events are queryable (see no-alerting-observability). No user-flow impact.
confirmed.verifier_note: Confirmed. No logging: block in the compose file. app.ts:94 applies hono logger() to every request. origins.ts:17 has `console.log('check origin')`. The dashboard has console.log in session.ts:15 and :44, server.ts:11 and hooks.server.ts:156. app.ts also logs every auth redirect. Unrotated json-file logs are a real disk-fill risk, and rotation is a one-line change. The 'several GB/day' estimate is inflated. At 5-20 req/s, one ~100-byte line per request is about 40-170 MB/day, plus dashboard lines and a healthcheck line every 10s. It would take months to fill an 80 GB disk. Medium.
confirmed.fix_adjustment: Add the x-logging anchor with max-size 20m and max-file 5, or set it in daemon.json. Remove the console.log lines. Do not drop the hono access log entirely. It is the only request trace, and correlationId lines must stay for RUNBOOK. Skip the logger for /health and '/' (healthcheck noise) rather than sampling all 2xx.

confirmed.title: No error alerting or metrics: Sentry is hard-disabled for self-hosted, healthchecks only cover 2 of 5 containers
confirmed.location: apps/api/src/instrument.ts:13; docker-compose.deploy.yaml:34-45 (only redis+api have healthchecks), :11-163 (no SENTRY_*/QUEUE_DASHBOARD_PASSWORD passed); docs/RUNBOOK.md:19-31
confirmed.current: Sentry.init only runs when `!isSelfHosted`, and prod is PUBLIC_IS_SELFHOSTED=true, so SENTRY_DSN is ignored. The deploy compose does not even pass SENTRY_*, PUBLIC_SENTRY_*, or QUEUE_DASHBOARD_PASSWORD into the containers. Alerting is a DO Uptime check on the login page and /health (owner action, 'pending'), and /health is deliberately dependency-free so a Redis/DB outage still reports healthy. The dashboard, jobs and caddy have no healthcheck. `restart: unless-stopped` restarts only on process exit, never for a hung but alive process. There are no queue-depth, DB-pool or latency signals.
confirmed.breaks_at: At scale the first signal of a problem will be learners emailing: stuck BullMQ queues (media/emails), a saturated Supabase pool, a hung dashboard, or exhausted Redis are all invisible. Mean-time-to-detect is dominated by humans.
confirmed.fix: (1) Allow Sentry when a DSN is set explicitly (gate on SENTRY_DSN plus an opt-in env, not on !selfHosted), set tracesSampleRate about 0.05, and pass SENTRY_DSN/PUBLIC_SENTRY_DSN through compose (self-hosted-compatible; Sentry free/Team tier). (2) Add a `/ready` endpoint (cheap `select 1` with 1 s timeout, redis PING) for the compose healthcheck, keep `/health` for liveness. (3) Add healthchecks: dashboard (`node -e fetch('http://localhost:3082/')`), jobs (a heartbeat key in Redis refreshed by a timer and checked by a script), caddy (`caddy validate`/admin API). (4) Add `willfarrell/autoheal` or a systemd timer to restart `unhealthy` containers. (5) Expose queue depth (BullMQ getJobCounts) on an authenticated metrics route, or mount the Workbench by setting QUEUE_DASHBOARD_PASSWORD, and alert on failed/waiting counts. (6) DO monitoring alerts for CPU>80%, memory>85%, disk>80%.
confirmed.flow_risk: Turning Sentry on must keep sendDefaultPii:false and avoid replay (the replay sample rate defaults to 1 in the dashboard, which would capture learner screens; set it to 0). Adding `/ready` DB checks into the container healthcheck can cause restart flapping during a Supabase blip, so keep a long retries window and do NOT let autoheal act on /ready, only on liveness. No functional flow impact.
confirmed.verifier_note: Mostly confirmed. instrument.ts only inits Sentry when `!isSelfHosted`, and prod is self-hosted. hooks.client.ts has the same gate. Compose passes no SENTRY_* or QUEUE_DASHBOARD_PASSWORD. Only redis and api have healthchecks. /health is deliberately dependency-free, and the api's own healthcheck hits '/', which is also dependency-free. Correction: the claim that the dashboard's replay sample rate 'defaults to 1' is wrong. replaysSessionSampleRate defaults to 0 and only replaysOnErrorSampleRate defaults to 1. Replay-on-error still captures sessions around errors, so set it to 0 anyway if Sentry is enabled. Medium: this is detection latency, not a correctness break.
confirmed.fix_adjustment: Keep it light. Gate Sentry on SENTRY_DSN plus an explicit opt-in env, keep sendDefaultPii false, and set a low trace rate. Add a /ready endpoint for monitoring only. Do not wire /ready into a container healthcheck or autoheal, to avoid restart flapping on Supabase blips. Prioritise DO monitoring alerts, the uptime check (already pending with the owner), and a dashboard healthcheck.

confirmed.title: Redis has no maxmemory/eviction policy and persists hot rate-limit churn to AOF
confirmed.current: Redis shares one instance and one unlimited memory pool across BullMQ queues, the per-request rate-limit sorted sets (4 commands per request, MULTI), analytics caches and OAuth handoffs. There is no maxmemory, no maxmemory-policy (BullMQ wants noeviction), no AOF rewrite sizing, and no container limit. Job retention is bounded (removeOnComplete/Fail age+count), which is good, but keys from emails/notifications fan-out are unbounded in burst.
confirmed.breaks_at: At thousands of users, rate-limit ZSETs hold up to 100-500 members per active user and rewrite AOF on every request. The AOF grows and rewrites steadily (disk I/O on a shared droplet disk). A burst of announcement emails or notifications queues many jobs. Without maxmemory, Redis grows into the OOM killer and takes the queue with it.
confirmed.fix: `redis-server --appendonly yes --appendfsync everysec --maxmemory 256mb --maxmemory-policy noeviction --auto-aof-rewrite-percentage 100 --auto-aof-rewrite-min-size 64mb` with mem_limit 320m. Better, separate concerns at 5k+ learners: one Redis for BullMQ (persistent) and one ephemeral Redis (`--save '' --appendonly no`, allkeys-lru) for rate limits and caches. Alert on used_memory > 70%.
confirmed.flow_risk: With noeviction, hitting maxmemory makes writes fail: the rate limiter already fails open (rate-limiter.ts:97-100) but job enqueue from the API would error, affecting uploads that trigger media jobs and notification/email fan-out for tutors and learners. Size generously and alert before the limit. Do not use an LRU policy on the BullMQ instance.
confirmed.verifier_note: The facts are true: `redis-server --appendonly yes` with no maxmemory and no container limit. But the impact is overstated. Job retention is bounded (removeOnComplete/Fail age and count in defaults.ts). Rate-limit ZSETs expire per window. AOF is append-only with the default auto-rewrite, so it does not 'rewrite on every request'. Redis 7 defaults to noeviction, which is what BullMQ needs. Memory will stay small for a long time. Low, and mostly a safety net.
confirmed.fix_adjustment: Setting maxmemory is fine, but size it generously (512mb or more) with a container limit above it. At maxmemory with noeviction, BullMQ enqueue from the api fails (upload and email fan-out), while the rate limiter fails open. Alert on used_memory rather than relying on the cap. Never use an LRU policy on the BullMQ instance. The two-Redis split is premature below several thousand learners.

confirmed.title: When Redis is slow/down every API request waits up to 2 s on the rate-limit check
confirmed.current: The global limiter runs on every non-trusted request (`app.ts:154`). It awaits `multi.exec()` under a 2 s `withTimeout` and then fails open. node-redis queues commands while disconnected (offline queue enabled, reconnect delay up to 3 s), so during a Redis restart (deploy, OOM, AOF load at boot) each browser request is delayed about 2 s before proceeding, and pending commands pile up in memory. `docker compose up` restarts also make api start `connectRedis` with no retry limit and no circuit breaker.
confirmed.breaks_at: A Redis blip of 30 s with 200 concurrent users adds 2 s to every request and queues thousands of commands per second in the API process, which can balloon memory and stack up inflight requests on a 4 GB box. A pure latency incident that looks like a site-wide slowdown.
confirmed.fix: Add a circuit breaker: after 1-2 consecutive limiter failures, skip the limiter for 10-30 s (cache `redisHealthy=false` using the client's `ready`/`end` events, which are already tracked as `isConnected`). Short-circuit when `!redis.isReady` instead of queuing. Set `disableOfflineQueue: true` for the rate-limiter client, or use a dedicated client for it. Lower the timeout to 250-500 ms.
confirmed.flow_risk: Failing open longer means brute-force protection on sign-in (the per-IP limit) is briefly absent during Redis outages. Better Auth has its own in-memory sign-in throttle as a backstop (auth.ts:132-141). Keep the sign-in and password-reset limiter fail-closed or stricter than the global one. All roles are only affected by latency, so this removes the worst impact.
confirmed.verifier_note: Confirmed. rate-limiter.ts uses a 2000 ms withTimeout then fails open. redis.ts sets no disableOfflineQueue (node-redis default is enabled), and reconnectStrategy retries forever, so commands queue while Redis is down. The rate limiter is global (`.use('*', rateLimiter)` at app.ts:154). Redis is local on the same box and only goes down during compose restarts or crashes, so the event is rare and short. Low to medium.
confirmed.fix_adjustment: The fix is safe: short-circuit when `!redis.isReady` and cut the timeout to about 300-500 ms. Keep a stricter or fail-closed limit for sign-in. Note that Better Auth's in-memory limiter is the only backstop there.

confirmed.title: API and dashboard have no drain on SIGTERM; jobs workers race each other on shutdown
confirmed.location: apps/api/src/index.ts:22-37; docker/entrypoint-api.sh:13; apps/jobs/src/workers/media.ts:83-91; apps/jobs/src/workers/emails.ts:66-74; apps/jobs/src/workers/maintenance.ts:147-157; apps/jobs/src/bootstrap.ts:103-109; docker-compose.deploy.yaml (no stop_grace_period)
confirmed.current: The api discards the `serve()` return value and registers no SIGTERM/SIGINT handlers, so in-flight requests (uploads, marking saves, SSE agent streams) are cut when `docker stop` times out (10 s) and SIGKILLs. The entrypoint does `exec pnpm --filter @cio/api start`, so PID 1 is pnpm with node as a child, and whether the signal reaches node depends on pnpm. In jobs, each of 6 workers registers its own SIGTERM handler that calls `process.exit(0)` after its own `worker.close()`, so the first worker to finish kills the process while others (for example a media job mid-ffmpeg or an email send) are still draining. Docker's default stop grace is 10 s, far below a media job. uncaughtException in jobs only logs and keeps running.
confirmed.breaks_at: Every deploy or restart interrupts some active requests and jobs. With many tutors and learners online during working hours, each deploy loses submissions-in-flight and creates stalled BullMQ jobs that must wait for the stalled-check interval (about 30 s) and retry, producing duplicate emails or duplicate notification fan-out where the processors are not idempotent.
confirmed.fix: api: `const server = serve(...)`; on SIGTERM call `server.close()` with a 25 s deadline, then `process.exit`. Change the entrypoint to `exec node apps/api/dist/index.js` (or use tini, `init: true`) so node is PID 1 and receives the signal. Set `stop_grace_period: 60s` on api and dashboard and `300s` on jobs (adapter-node honours SHUTDOWN_TIMEOUT, so set it to 30). In jobs, replace the six per-file handlers with one central shutdown that closes ALL workers/connections in parallel (Promise.allSettled) and exits once, with a bounded timeout. Make uncaughtException in jobs exit non-zero so Docker restarts a known state.
confirmed.flow_risk: Draining holds the old container up to the grace period, which lengthens deploy time slightly. SSE/long-lived agent streams will be force-closed at the deadline. Ensure processors are idempotent (emails dedupe key) because a long ffmpeg job cut at 300 s is still retried. Affects learner submission and tutor marking flows positively.
confirmed.verifier_note: Confirmed on every point. api index.ts discards serve()'s return value and has no signal handlers. entrypoint-api.sh does `exec pnpm --filter @cio/api start`, so pnpm is PID 1. The jobs workers (media, media-transcribe, emails, notifications, maintenance, agent-course-generation) each register their own SIGTERM handler that ends in process.exit(0), so the first to finish kills the others mid-job. bootstrap.ts uncaughtException only logs. No stop_grace_period is set, so Docker's 10 s default applies. Stalled jobs are retried by BullMQ after the stalled check. Real, medium.
confirmed.fix_adjustment: Use one central jobs shutdown that closes all workers with Promise.allSettled, then exits once. Set stop_grace_period to about 60s on api and dashboard and 120-300s on jobs. Make the api exec `node` directly, or use init: true. Make email and notification processors idempotent before relying on retries. The dashboard runs `node build/index.js` directly, so adapter-node already handles SIGTERM, and it only needs the grace period.

confirmed.title: Dashboard proxy buffers whole request bodies in memory and BODY_SIZE_LIMIT allows 25 MB on every route
confirmed.current: `init.body = await request.arrayBuffer()` reads the entire /proxy and /api/auth request into a Node buffer before forwarding. BODY_SIZE_LIMIT=26214400 (25 MB) applies to the entire dashboard app, and Caddy has no request_body max_size and no per-route limit. Responses are streamed (fine), but requests are not. The dashboard is a single Node process.
confirmed.breaks_at: Concurrent profile/cover/logo uploads (and any malicious or buggy client posting 25 MB to any /proxy route) multiply: 40 concurrent 25 MB bodies is 1 GB+ transient (arrayBuffer plus the undici copy), on a 4 GB shared host with no container cap. This can pause the single event loop with GC and OOM-kill the dashboard, taking every user's SSR down. It scales with the number of users uploading avatars at the start of a cohort.
confirmed.fix: (1) Stream instead of buffering: `init.body = request.body; init.duplex = 'half'` (Node 20 fetch supports it). (2) In Caddy, add `request_body { max_size 1MB }` globally and a `@uploads path /proxy/media/*` matcher with `max_size 26MB`; keep adapter-node's BODY_SIZE_LIMIT as defense in depth. (3) Move image uploads to presigned direct-to-Supabase uploads like documents/videos already do, which removes the droplet from the data path entirely.
confirmed.flow_risk: Streaming bodies cannot be retried on 307/308 or connection reset (fetch with a stream body can't replay), and `redirect: 'manual'` is already used. Test the Better Auth POSTs (/api/auth/sign-in, change-password) and multipart uploads specifically. A too-low Caddy max_size would break admin logo/cover uploads and tutor avatar crops (UPLOAD_MAX_IMAGE_MB defaults to 5), so keep headroom above 5 MB multipart overhead. Learners and tutors using only JSON endpoints are unaffected.
confirmed.verifier_note: Confirmed. proxy-api-request.ts:141-143 does `init.body = await request.arrayBuffer()`. Compose sets BODY_SIZE_LIMIT 26214400 for the whole dashboard, and Caddy has no request_body limit. /api/auth/* is unauthenticated, so any client can force 25 MB buffers through a single Node process. That is a real memory-DoS lever. But 40 concurrent 25 MB legitimate uploads is unrealistic. The api image limit is 5 MB, and documents and videos use presigned direct uploads. The risk is an abusive client, not organic growth. Medium, not high.
confirmed.fix_adjustment: Streaming with `duplex:'half'` is the right fix. Test the Better Auth POSTs and multipart image uploads. Inventory every /proxy route that takes a body before adding a global Caddy cap such as 1 MB. A global cap would break image upload, plus any docx, CSV or import endpoints that go through the proxy. Use per-path matchers: a small cap on /api/auth/* and a 26 MB cap on the media upload paths.

confirmed.title: Better Auth sign-in/reset throttles use per-process memory; custom-domain origin registry is per-process: not replica-safe, reset on every deploy
confirmed.current: The `rateLimit.customRules` block does not configure `storage` (or secondaryStorage), so Better Auth defaults to an in-memory store for the sign-in, forget-password and request-password-reset limits. Each process has its own counters, and they reset on every container restart. The verified custom-domain origin registry is preloaded into process memory at boot and trust/untrust only updates the local process. The global limiter (Redis ZSET) is already shared.
confirmed.breaks_at: With 2+ api replicas, the effective sign-in limit is N times the configured one, and an attacker only needs a deploy-restart or a second replica to reset counters. Domain registrations made through one replica are not visible on the others until restart. Not a problem with one replica, but a blocker for the scale-out path.
confirmed.fix: Set `rateLimit.storage: 'secondary-storage'` and wire `secondaryStorage` to the existing node-redis client (get/set with TTL/delete), which also lets session cookies' backing be cached in Redis. Alternatively put the sign-in/reset limits into the Redis-based createRateLimiter on those routes. For the origin registry, fall back to a short-TTL Redis/DB lookup or a pub/sub invalidate. If custom domains are inert in this self-hosted deployment, document and disable the preload.
confirmed.flow_risk: Secondary storage adds Redis on the login path, so sign-in depends on Redis health: reuse the fail-open pattern with a timeout so a Redis outage cannot lock everyone out. Wrong key prefixes could collide with existing `rate_limit:` keys. All roles log in through this path, so test admin, tutor, learner and manager sign-in, password reset and /get-session behaviour (already exempt).
confirmed.verifier_note: Confirmed. auth.ts:132-141 sets rateLimit.customRules with no storage config, so Better Auth uses its in-memory default. The origin registry is preloaded per process. With one api replica this is harmless, and counters resetting on deploy is minor. It only matters once the api is scaled out. Low today, but a prerequisite for replicas.
confirmed.fix_adjustment: Danger in the proposed fix: wiring Better Auth `secondaryStorage` to Redis also moves SESSION storage into Redis by default, unless `session.storeSessionInDatabase` is true. That would change session behaviour, log users out, and affect anything reading the session table. Use a rate-limit-only store instead (`rateLimit.storage`/`customStorage`, if the installed Better Auth version supports it; verify). Otherwise put the sign-in and reset limits on the existing Redis createRateLimiter. Keep it fail-open with a timeout.

confirmed.title: Tuning/ops env vars documented in ENV.md are not passed by the deploy compose, so they cannot be changed without editing the file and rebuilding
confirmed.current: The compose passes a fixed whitelist of vars. DATABASE_POOL_MAX (default 10 per process; `|| 5` only if NaN), MEDIA/TRANSCRIBE/EMAIL/AGENT worker concurrency, QUEUE_DASHBOARD_PASSWORD, SENTRY_*, BODY limits for the API, SHUTDOWN_TIMEOUT, NODE_OPTIONS and OPENAI_API_KEY for the API are all absent, so setting them in the droplet `.env` has no effect. Pool max is therefore fixed at 10 per process for api, 10 for jobs, with no dashboard DB use. The Supabase pooler client limit is not recorded, and a rolling deploy doubles connections.
confirmed.breaks_at: When a second api replica or a bigger Supabase compute tier is added, connection math (10 x replicas x services plus the migrate connection and the advisory-lock connection) can exceed the pooler's client limit or the Supabase 'auth_db_connections_absolute' warning. Operators cannot react by editing `.env`, so tuning requires a code-level deploy at the worst time.
confirmed.fix: Add pass-through lines `DATABASE_POOL_MAX: ${DATABASE_POOL_MAX:-10}`, `*_WORKER_CONCURRENCY: ${...}`, `QUEUE_DASHBOARD_PASSWORD`, `SENTRY_DSN`, `SENTRY_TRACES_SAMPLE_RATE`, `NODE_OPTIONS`, `SHUTDOWN_TIMEOUT` to the right services and list them in .env.deploy.example. Document the connection budget in DEPLOY.md: total = replicas x pool max, kept under about 60-70% of the Supabase pooler limit, and keep the direct 5432 connections for migrations only.
confirmed.flow_risk: Defaults preserve today's behaviour, so nothing changes until a value is set. Lowering the pool max too far serialises DB calls across all roles; raising it risks pooler exhaustion for everyone. Change one knob at a time and watch the Supabase pooler metrics.
confirmed.verifier_note: Confirmed. The compose environment whitelist omits DATABASE_POOL_MAX, the worker concurrency variables, QUEUE_DASHBOARD_PASSWORD, SENTRY_*, SHUTDOWN_TIMEOUT and NODE_OPTIONS. drizzle.ts:24 reads DATABASE_POOL_MAX with a default of 10. Defaults mean nothing is broken today, so the severity is low. Correction: the Supabase advisor `auth_db_connections_absolute` concerns Supabase's own Auth server connection allocation, not this app's pool, so do not tie it to this pool math.
confirmed.fix_adjustment: Pass-through lines with the current defaults are zero-risk. Also document the connection budget. Current peak is api 10 + jobs 10 + a temporary db-setup connection set. A rolling deploy briefly doubles api and jobs connections.

confirmed.title: Retention/cleanup jobs never run: dead-letter cleanup unscheduled, retention-compact is a no-op
confirmed.current: `deadLetterCleanup` and `retentionCompact` handlers exist but only three schedulers are registered (media-job-reap every 5 min, analytics-rollup daily, system-event purge daily). `retentionCompact` explicitly logs `retention-compact-noop` ('not-yet-implemented') for media_job, job_step and email_delivery. system_event_log retention is 90 days, but api.error rows are written for every 4xx AppError (app.ts:328) and 500.
confirmed.breaks_at: dead_letter_job, media_job, job_step, email_delivery and system_event_log (every handled 4xx is a row, each costing a pooled DB connection) grow unbounded. By thousands of learners x years these become the biggest tables and slow the rollup and admin screens. A 4xx/5xx storm (expired sessions, a bad deploy) turns into a burst of DB inserts on the same 10-connection pool as the request path.
confirmed.fix: Register schedulers for deadLetterCleanup (daily, 30-60 d) and a real retentionCompact with batched DELETE (LIMIT 5k loops) for email_delivery/job_step/media_job older than N days, plus pruning expired `session` and `verification` rows (Better Auth does not delete them on its own). In app.ts:onError, skip DB writes for 401/403/404 (keep for 5xx) or sample and batch via a Redis list flushed by the maintenance worker. Add a ceiling on rows/second.
confirmed.flow_risk: Deleting anything referenced by audit/progress screens would break tutor marking history or learner timelines, so scope retention strictly to operational tables (not coursework_*/audit_event) and confirm with the data owner first (data must not be changed without explicit approval). Never delete rows with an in-progress status. Large deletes on a live table need batching to avoid lock/IO spikes.
confirmed.verifier_note: Confirmed. Only three schedulers are registered (media-job-reap, analytics-daily-rollup, system-event-purge). deadLetterCleanup has a handler but no scheduler. retentionCompact logs `retention-compact-noop`. recordApiError writes a system_event_log row for every AppError below 500 (app.ts:65-89, :320). Growth is real but slow. Event purge exists at 90 days, and a 4xx row is a fire-and-forget insert. This is housekeeping, not a scale blocker. Low.
confirmed.fix_adjustment: Schedule deadLetterCleanup first, since it is trivial and safe. Scope any retention to operational tables only (never coursework, audit or progress tables). Batch deletes, and get owner approval before deleting data. Skip DB writes for expected 401/403/404 rather than sampling. Pruning expired session and verification rows is reasonable but I did not verify it.

confirmed.title: Migrations and seed run on every api boot inside the app container; drizzle migrate runs in one transaction so zero-lock index builds are impossible
confirmed.current: Each api start takes a session-level advisory lock on the direct connection, runs baseline plus `drizzle-kit migrate`, then re-seeds essential reference data (roles, submissions, question types) on every restart (db-setup.ts:111). drizzle's migrator applies all pending migrations in a single transaction, so `CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY` can't be used. The 103 unindexed FKs and any new indexes will be plain CREATE INDEX, which blocks writes on that table while it builds. A crash-looping api re-runs all of this each restart.
confirmed.breaks_at: Today tables are small (7 submissions, ~40 learners) so index builds are instant. At 20k learners, indexing coursework_result, session or audit tables takes tens of seconds to minutes with writes blocked, while the new api container is not yet healthy and the old one is already stopped. Marking and submission writes stall for that period.
confirmed.fix: Move migration into the separate one-shot `migrate` service (see no-zero-downtime-deploy) and run the FK-index backlog NOW, while the tables are tiny, as one reviewed migration (or via the Supabase SQL editor with CONCURRENTLY). For later large-table indexes, use a non-transactional runner (psql -f with `CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY IF NOT EXISTS`) as a pre-deploy step. Seed only when a migration changed (hash check) or behind a flag. Set `lock_timeout` / `statement_timeout` in db-setup so a blocked migration fails fast instead of hanging boot.
confirmed.flow_risk: Pure DDL ordering; the key risk is a migration that renames/drops a column the still-running old code uses (needs expand/contract). Seeding less often could leave new reference rows (roles, question types) missing if a release adds them, so key the seed on a version marker. Index creation now is harmless to all roles; it speeds tutor-scoped queries (tutor_allocation joins).
confirmed.verifier_note: Confirmed. db-setup.ts:96-114 takes an advisory lock and runs the baseline plus runMigrations() on every api boot, then runSeedEssential() unconditionally. The drizzle migrator runs pending migrations in one transaction, so CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY cannot be used inside it. The plain CREATE INDEX on a large table blocks writes. Today's tables are tiny, so the 103-FK index backlog is cheap now and costly later. Doing it now is the most valuable action in this finding.
confirmed.fix_adjustment: Ship the reviewed FK-index migration NOW while tables are small, as plain CREATE INDEX IF NOT EXISTS. Keep migrations expand/contract. Add lock_timeout and statement_timeout to db-setup. Key the seed on a version marker so new reference rows are never skipped. Moving migrations to a one-shot service is a deploy change that overlaps with no-zero-downtime-deploy.

confirmed.title: Backups: object storage has no independent copy, restore drill never executed, droplet has no backup or IaC for caddy-data
confirmed.current: Database durability relies on Supabase PITR/daily backups that are an 'owner confirms' item, and the restore drill row is 'pending owner scratch project'. Supabase database backups do not include Storage object bytes, only metadata. Coursework .docx and lesson attachments live in the private `documents` bucket, and RUNBOOK says to implement an off-site export 'only if the owner asks'. The droplet has 'no DO backups'. State on the droplet is caddy-data (Let's Encrypt account/certs), redis-data (queue/rate limit state) and the checked-out git repo plus a hand-made `.env`, and the `.env` secrets exist only on that box.
confirmed.breaks_at: With thousands of learners submitting coursework, accidental bucket deletion, a bad cleanup job (assetStorageCleanup runs purgeAssetStorage) or a Supabase incident means unrecoverable learner evidence (assessment/regulatory risk). Rebuilding the droplet from scratch without a saved .env means regenerating BETTER_AUTH_SECRET, which invalidates every session and may break encrypted data.
confirmed.fix: (1) Confirm PITR on and run the restore drill once now; record the timing. (2) Nightly `rclone sync`/`aws s3 sync` of `documents` (and `videos` if needed) from Supabase S3 to a second provider (Backblaze B2/DO Spaces ~ $5-10/mo for 500 GB), run from the jobs container as a maintenance scheduler or a host cron, with versioning or lifecycle rules. (3) Enable DO droplet backups (20% of the plan price, about $4.80/mo). (4) Store the production `.env` in a secrets manager or encrypted vault copy (1Password/age), and snapshot caddy-data weekly.
confirmed.flow_risk: Read-only sync doesn't touch live flows, but it adds egress and API calls against the Supabase storage S3 endpoint (already noted as hot, 166k storage.objects lookups): schedule off-peak and throttle with rclone `--tpslimit`. Keep the backup bucket credentials separate from the app's write keys.
confirmed.verifier_note: Confirmed from RUNBOOK.md §3-4: PITR and daily backups are 'owner confirms', the restore drill is pending, and storage objects rely on Supabase Storage's own durability with no independent copy. Supabase database backups do not contain Storage object bytes, which is a known limitation. Coursework documents are regulatory evidence, so this gap is worth high. The droplet-side items (.env only on the box, caddy-data) are lower. Caddy can reissue certs. The .env is the real single point of loss.
confirmed.fix_adjustment: Confirm PITR and run the drill. Take an off-site nightly copy of the documents bucket with throttling (rclone --tpslimit) and separate credentials. Store a copy of the production .env in a vault. DO droplet backups at about 20% are cheap. Pricing figures are unverified list prices.

confirmed.title: Single-stage, root-running images ship full monorepo + dev deps + pnpm store; old images accumulate on the droplet disk
confirmed.current: Each Dockerfile is one stage: `COPY . .`, a full `pnpm install` (api uses --shamefully-hoist), build, then runs from that same layer, so the runtime image contains the pnpm store (/pnpm/store), TypeScript and build tooling, sources, and for the api the `tsx` and pnpm needed by db:setup. There is no USER directive (everything runs as root), no HEALTHCHECK in the images, and dashboard Dockerfile has EXPOSE 3000 while the app is on 3082. Every deploy builds new multi-GB images for 3 services; cleanup is a manual 'docker image prune'.
confirmed.breaks_at: Each deploy adds ~3-9 GB of image layers; on an 80 GB droplet that also holds logs and the Docker overlay, a few weeks of deploys without pruning fills the disk and breaks the next build or the running containers. Larger images also slow pull-based deploys (once CI builds are introduced) and increase the attack surface of a root process.
confirmed.fix: Convert to multi-stage builds (builder -> `pnpm deploy --prod --filter` or copy only `dist` plus prod node_modules into a slim runner), run as `USER node`, set `init: true` (tini) in compose, and fix the EXPOSE. Keep pnpm and tsx only in the migrate image. Add `docker image prune -af --filter until=168h` to a weekly cron and a DO disk alert at 80%. Expect images to shrink to ~400-700 MB.
confirmed.flow_risk: Dropping devDependencies or hoisting can break runtime requires that currently work by accident (the api uses --shamefully-hoist, workspace packages exported as TS/dist). Verify with the smoke test (boot each image against postgres+redis) before cutover. Running as non-root needs write access to os.tmpdir() (/tmp is fine) for ffmpeg temp dirs in jobs. No functional change for any role if the smoke test passes.
confirmed.verifier_note: Confirmed. All three Dockerfiles are single-stage with COPY . ., a full install and the build in the final image. No USER directive and no HEALTHCHECK. Dockerfile.dashboard has EXPOSE 3000 and PORT 3000 baked in, but compose overrides PORT to 3082, so that is cosmetic. .dockerignore exists. Image size mainly costs disk and pull time, and docker layer cache reuse means growth per deploy is less than the 3-9 GB claimed. Low until images are pulled from a registry.
confirmed.fix_adjustment: Defer. Do it after CI-built images exist. Multi-stage plus --prod pruning is risky in this monorepo (workspace packages, tsx and pnpm are needed for db:setup, and the api uses --shamefully-hoist). Gate it behind the smoke test. A weekly `docker image prune` cron is the cheap interim fix.

confirmed.title: Staged infra path and rough monthly cost deltas (what to do now vs 1k / 5k / 20k learners)
confirmed.current: Everything (caddy, dashboard SSR, api, jobs/ffmpeg, redis) shares one s-2vcpu-4gb droplet ($24/mo) in lon1. Postgres and storage are on Supabase (cvtmymxxjgjshrzsjxnj). There is one replica of everything, the droplet is a single point of failure, and the dashboard SSR plus the api HTTP hop do session resolution per page.
confirmed.breaks_at: CPU is the first limit: dashboard SSR is single-threaded Node and the api is a second Node process. 2 vCPU also has to host ffmpeg. Expect pain around several hundred concurrently active users, earlier when a media job or a deploy-build runs. Memory is the second limit (4 GB shared, no caps). Supabase pooler/compute is third (pool 10 per process, 103 unindexed FKs, hundreds of thousands of redundant org/plan lookups already).
confirmed.fix: NOW (<=1k learners, +$0-6/mo): CI-built images on GHCR (free), logging rotation, memory limits, swap, split jobs-media, Redis maxmemory, healthchecks/autoheal, /ready, Sentry (free tier), DO monitoring alerts, nightly storage export (about +$5), droplet backups (+$4.80), fix redundant per-request org/plan DB lookups and index the FKs (code/DB side, $0). Cloudflare free proxy/CDN in front of Caddy for static /_app/immutable assets (lowers droplet CPU and bandwidth; $0). 1k-5k learners (about +$30-90/mo): move to s-4vcpu-8gb ($48, +$24) or Premium CPU-optimized, run 2 dashboard + 2 api replicas with the rollout pattern, separate the jobs-media container, Supabase Pro compute upgrade Small/Medium (+$15 to +$60 over base Pro $25), a 2nd small droplet for jobs/ffmpeg only ($12-24) so media never competes with SSR. 5k-20k learners (about +$150-350/mo): 2 app droplets (s-4vcpu-8gb x2, about $96) behind a DO Load Balancer ($12) or Cloudflare LB, managed Valkey/Redis ($15-30) for shared rate-limit/BullMQ, dedicated worker droplet (c-4 CPU-optimized, about $42-84), Supabase Large compute ($110) with read-replica considered for reporting, CDN for media, log/metrics stack (Grafana Cloud free or about $20). Decision triggers: p95 SSR > 800 ms, CPU > 70% sustained, memory > 80%, queue wait > 60 s, Supabase pooler > 60% of the client limit.
confirmed.flow_risk: Each step is additive to the previous one. Scale-out requires the stateless fixes above (Better Auth rate-limit storage in Redis, shared origin registry, graceful shutdown, DNS/LB for dashboard to api calls). A load balancer must forward the real client IP (Caddy/CF header trust is hard-coded: ipAddressHeaders x-forwarded-for, and proxy-api-request.ts:128-133 trusts only XFF), otherwise per-IP sign-in throttles collapse to one bucket or become spoofable (auth.ts:128-131 notes this).
